title: The deer and the fire-sticks
hookLine: a deer runs off with a brahmin's fire-sticks, the Pandavas chase it to save his sacred fire, and a voice at a lake says: answer first
carry: agni carries the offering to the gods

cards: A pair of fire-sticks, swinging from a deer's antlers. A brahmin comes running to the Pandavas in their forest exile.

He had left his arani, the two pieces of wood he rubs together to kindle his sacred fire, hanging on a tree. A deer rubbed against the tree, the sticks caught in its antlers, and now it's bounding away with them.
Without them, he can't keep his fire. The five brothers take up their bows and go after it, deeper into the trees than any of them meant to go.

teach.b: Why would five princes risk their lives for two sticks of wood? Because of what the sticks make. In the Vedas, Agni, the god of fire, is the messenger who carries offerings up to the gods.

A Vedic householder kept a sacred fire, and kindled it by rubbing the arani together. Without them, the brahmin can't kindle his sacred fire, his line to the gods. Protecting it is a king's dharma, so the brothers run.

teach.h: FIRE AT THE HEART OF HINDU LIFE.
teach.b: And that fire is still at the center of Hindu life. At a wedding the couple walk around a fire, with Agni as their witness. When a family moves into a new home, a priest often lights a havan in the living room.
But the deer stays just out of reach. They shoot and miss, and it's gone.

teach.h: THE DEER ESCAPES. NAKULA SEEKS WATER.
teach.b: Parched, they sink down under a tree, and Yudhishthira sends Nakula to climb it and look for water. Nakula sees green plants and cranes, and goes alone. He finds a lake, clear and still.
He is about to drink when a voice speaks from nowhere. Don't be rash, child. This lake is mine.
Answer my questions first, then drink. Nakula is burning with thirst.
He kneels, drinks, and falls down dead on the bank. The questions haven't been asked yet.

how: The Yaksha's questions are a dialogue on dharma set in the Pandavas' forest years, and the episode opens with the brothers' chase to recover a brahmin's arani, the fire-sticks for his sacred fire.

practice: If you have a diya or a candle, light it and set it where you can see it; if not, picture one. Watch the flame for a few breaths. Many Hindu homes light a lamp like this every morning or evening.
Think of one thing you'd like to offer today: a kind word, an hour of work, a meal shared. If you pray, offer it into the flame in your own words; if not, simply set your intention by the light.

wordCard.voice: Arani, the fire-sticks that kindle a sacred fire, carried off on a deer's antlers. Five brothers chase them for a brahmin's fire, and one brother drinks before he listens. Today's word.
